title: She still gave
hookLine: Suppavasa, in a long and hard pregnancy, still gives; she is safely delivered
tomorrow: A hundred dear, a hundred sorrows

lines: A VERY LONG, VERY HARD WAIT.
cards: A hospital waiting room. The coffee goes cold. The clock seems broken.

Every time the door opens, every head looks up. The Udana tells of Suppavasa, a Koliyan noblewoman, whose wait the text measures in years. It says she carried her child for seven years, and was in labor for seven days.
Readers take those numbers in different ways; what's plain is a very long, very hard wait. And in the middle of it, she does something unexpected.

teach.b: In her pain, the text says, Suppavasa holds on to three thoughts. The Buddha teaches the way out of suffering like this. His community practices that way.

And there is a peace where suffering like this doesn't exist. The teacher, the community, the peace, held in labor. She sends her husband to bow at the Buddha's feet in her name and tell him how she is.
The Buddha says: may Suppavasa be well and free from illness, and give birth to a healthy son. And at that moment, the text says, she does. Then the part the title is about.
As soon as she's able, she sends her husband back to invite the Buddha and the monks for meals, seven days in a row. She has just come through seven days of labor, and her first wish is to give.
The Buddha even asks her: would you want another child like this one? Yes, she says, she would have seven more.

teach.h: PAIN IN THE FORM OF HAPPINESS.
teach.b: The verse that follows is surprising: what is unpleasant comes disguised as pleasant, the hateful as dear, pain in the form of happiness, and overwhelms the heedless.
Readers take it in different ways; some hear the Buddha seeing her joy and her pain held together. Tradition says the child grew up to be the monk Sivali, remembered for how freely gifts came to him.

how: In some Theravada communities families invite monks for a meal and a blessing around a birth, and protective chants are sometimes recited for women in childbirth.

o: a fee paid to a teacher

games.q: she still gave: tap the pairs.

of meals for the Buddha and monks

s: Suppavasa went to the Buddha herself while in labor
she sent her husband to bow in her name.
after the birth she invited the Buddha and monks for seven days of meals
her first wish, once she was able, was to give.
asked if she'd want another child like this, she said no
she said she would have seven more.

games.q: you're Suppavasa. after seven days of labor, you've given birth safely. what do you do first, in the Udana?
o: invite the Buddha and monks to seven days of meals.
ask for a blessing for the child only.
games.why: she gives. it's why the day is called she still gave.

practice: Think of someone who is in a long wait right now, for a baby, a diagnosis, a visa, a phone call, and picture them where they are. Wish them well, the way the Buddha wished Suppavasa well: may you be well and free from illness.
Let the wish be quiet and plain, in your own words or none, and if you pray, hold them in your prayers.

wordCard.voice: Dana, giving. Suppavasa, after a long and terrible labor, invited the Buddha and the monks for seven days of meals. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dana: giving, generosity, the first of the perfections; Suppavasa's meals are dana.

carryVoice: Your line: give one small thing anyway. Fresh from seven days of labor, Suppavasa's first wish was to give. That's day six hundred twenty-one.
